title: 三億円の申し出  (Three Hundred Million Yen)

segments.t: At the jazz lounge booth, Ikezawa signals Mama-san and sets down a staggering pile of cash in front of Muranishi and Toshi: three hundred million yen. He offers to buy out all of Muranishi's Hokudai Kanda bookstores before they expand past Hokkaido and clash with him—only for Muranishi to bow politely and walk out. Listen to the high-stakes negotiation first without worrying about every detail.
ママ。
お前さんの店、俺にすべて買い取らせてくれないかな。
三億ある。これは手付金だ。
なぜうちを？
北大神田書店はこの先も拡大するよ。
当然、お前さんは販売網を北海道からさらに広げるわな？
そうなるとだ。
俺たちは不幸な形で出会ってしまう。
失礼します。あなたに会えてよかった。
行くぞ、トシ。
ちょっと待ってよ。
Even with three hundred million yen on the table, the threat and the refusal stay remarkably composed. Let's break down the key lines.
お前さんの店、俺にすべて買い取らせてくれないかな。

'Would you let me buy out all of your stores?' "Omaesan" softens rough "omae" into an older boss's folksy 'you'. "Subete" means all, and "kaitorasete" builds on "kaitoru", buy up, asking Muranishi to let him make the buyout.
三億ある。
'There is three hundred million yen here.' Japanese steps up to a fresh big-number unit at a hundred million, called "oku". Three of those—"san-oku"—makes three hundred million.
これは手付金だ。
'This is the deposit.' "Kore wa" points straight at the stack in front of them, and "tetsukekin" combines "te", hand, "tsuke", attaching, and "kin", money, for an earnest-money down payment.
なぜうちを？

'Why our company?' "Naze" is a crisp, slightly formal word for 'why'—steadier in business talk than everyday "doushite". "Uchi" again means 'our shop' or 'our side', marked with "o" as the target of the buyout.
北大神田書店はこの先も拡大するよ。
'Hokudai Kanda bookstores will keep expanding from here on.' "Kono saki mo" pairs "kono saki", ahead from here, with "mo", even further, while "kakudai suru" means to expand in scale.
当然、お前さんは販売網を北海道からさらに広げるわな？

'Naturally, you will expand your sales network even further beyond Hokkaido, right?' "Touzen" opens with 'naturally, of course'. "Hanbaimou" links "hanbai", sales, with "mou", net, and "hirogeru" means to spread or widen.
俺たちは不幸な形で出会ってしまう。

'We will end up meeting in an unfortunate way.' "Oretachi" adds plural "tachi" to masculine "ore" for 'us'. "Fukou na katachi", an unfortunate form, leads into "deatte shimau", where "shimau" adds a heavy sense of 'regrettably end up'.
失礼します。
'Excuse me for leaving.' Literally 'I am committing a rudeness', "shitsurei shimasu" is the standard polite line when excusing yourself from a meeting or leaving the room before a superior.
あなたに会えてよかった。
'I am glad I got to meet you.' Turning "au", meet, into "aete", 'able to meet', and adding "yokatta", 'was good', creates a warm, dignified farewell—even when turning a deal down flat.
行くぞ、トシ。
'Let us go, Toshi.' Back on his feet, Muranishi drops the polite polish: plain "iku", go, plus punchy masculine "zo" tells his partner they are walking out right now.
ちょっと待ってよ。

'Hey, wait up.' Staring at the cash left behind, Toshi calls out "chotto matte yo"—combining "matte", wait, from "matsu", with insistent "yo". Now let's hear the entire buyout offer and walkout again from start to finish.
ママ。
お前さんの店、俺にすべて買い取らせてくれないかな。
三億ある。これは手付金だ。
なぜうちを？
北大神田書店はこの先も拡大するよ。
当然、お前さんは販売網を北海道からさらに広げるわな？
そうなるとだ。
俺たちは不幸な形で出会ってしまう。
失礼します。あなたに会えてよかった。
行くぞ、トシ。
ちょっと待ってよ。
Remember "oku" for units of one hundred million, "shitsurei shimasu" for excusing yourself cleanly from a room, and "aete yokatta" to tell someone it was great meeting them. Goodbye until next time.
さようなら。
